title: A Proud Count and a Costly Altar
overview: David orders a count of his fighting men, a deadly plague follows, and the spot where it stops becomes holy ground in Jerusalem, later the site of the temple.

parts.label: David counts his army (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: The older telling in 2 Samuel 24 says the LORD's anger moved David, while this one says "satan," a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser, did it, and scholars debate how the two accounts fit together. The text never says exactly why the count was wrong, but many read it as pride or trust in military size, and even Joab, David's tough army chief, found it so wrong that he left out two tribes.

parts.label: Guilt and three choices (vv. 7-13)
parts.note: David admits he acted foolishly, and the prophet Gad brings him a grim choice of famine, war or plague. David chooses the plague because he would rather trust God's mercy than the mercy of human enemies.

parts.label: The plague stops at Jerusalem (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: Seventy thousand men die, and the text does not soften this, before God halts the angel just as it reaches Jerusalem. David and the leaders put on sackcloth, rough cloth worn in grief, and David asks that the punishment fall on him and his family rather than on the people.

parts.label: Buying Araunah's threshing floor (vv. 18-25)
parts.note: Araunah (also called Ornan) offers his threshing floor, a flat patch of ground where oxen dragged sledges over grain, along with his oxen and tools, all for free. David insists on paying because he will not give God an offering that costs him nothing, though 2 Samuel gives a much smaller price and it is unclear how the two accounts fit.

parts.label: Fire and a new holy place (vv. 26-30)
parts.note: Fire from heaven was a sign that God accepted the sacrifice, and the angel's sword is put away. The official place of worship, the tent Moses had made, was then at Gibeon, but the writer is showing why this spot in Jerusalem became the site of the temple, which a later passage links to Mount Moriah.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to reconcile this chapter's claim that the adversary incited David with 2 Samuel's claim that the LORD did, some seeing God allowing an evil act for his own purposes and others seeing two writers with different emphases telling the same event.
think: When a leader's choice brings harm on people who had no say in it, what do you think a real apology from that leader should look like?
